Topic: If you claim to kill in the name of justice, what prevents the next man from killing you in the name of his justice?
Montaigne — Judgement:
The question is not about justice but about the man who believes he possesses it — for I have observed that those most certain of their righteousness are most ready with the blade.

I lived through the Wars of Religion and watched my neighbors destroy one another, each side clutching the same God as their warrant, each calling the other's dead a necessary sacrifice. Justice, like custom, shifts with the longitude — what Persia calls holy, Portugal calls atrocity. The man who kills for justice has not reasoned his way to certainty; he has merely mistaken the clamor of his passion for the voice of God, and that error is the most murderous in history.

The license you seize to execute your enemy is the identical license he holds over you, and nothing in the universe distinguishes the two.

*Every executioner believes himself a judge, and every judge believes himself God.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
The question is not about justice at all — it is about the will that dresses itself in borrowed robes, mistaking the costume for the wearer.

Justice is not a river that flows from some celestial height; it is a weapon forged by those strong enough to forge it and weak enough to need the disguise. When a man kills "in the name of justice," he has already confessed his poverty: he cannot bear to act from his own will, so he borrows the authority of an abstraction he himself invented. What prevents the next man from doing likewise? Nothing — and that is precisely the exposure. The moment you invoke an external justice, you have surrendered the only ground you ever stood on. You have made yourself killable by your own logic.

Nothing protects the man who mortgages his will to a borrowed creed.

*He who kills for justice has already died for an illusion.*
Emerson — Judgement:
The question is not about violence but about the source of moral authority — whether justice can be a private possession of the self-asserting ego.

When I counsel self-reliance, I do not mean reliance upon the whims of wounded pride or tribal passion. I mean reliance upon that deeper Current which flows through all souls alike — what I have called the Over-Soul. The man who kills in the name of justice and the man who kills *him* in the name of his justice are both claiming the same throne. One is lying to himself. True moral sentiment, drawn from the universal source, does not contradict itself across two honest hearts; the contradiction reveals that at least one man has substituted appetite for conscience, custom for the soul's light.

Nothing external prevents the retaliatory blade. Only the quality of the inward act determines whether justice was done at all.

*Call no act just whose warrant you could not sign before God and your enemy both.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
The guillotine does not distinguish between the tyrant and the liberator once both have claimed the same sovereign authority over life. This is not a question of revolution — it is a question of what revolution becomes when power ceases to answer to the people.

When justice becomes the private property of the man holding the blade, it ceases to be justice and assumes its most elaborate disguise. I witnessed this in France — men who spoke liberty's name in January wearing liberty's blood on their hands by July. No cause, however righteous in origin, survives the moment its enforcers exempt themselves from the very rights they proclaim. Rights are not instruments of faction; they are either universal or they are merely the flattering name a stronger party gives to its appetites.

The chain of retributive murder has no natural terminus; it ends only when no one remains to avenge.

*He who makes himself the judge of all men has already sentenced himself.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The question names the precise catastrophe I spent my life warning against: private men erecting themselves as judges in their own cause, wielding the sword under the banner of conscience.

In the state of nature, every man's reason is sovereign to himself — and therefore no man's reason is sovereign at all. This is not freedom; it is the condition I named plainly: solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. When justice becomes a private weapon, it ceases to be justice and becomes merely appetite dressed in moral clothing. The covenant that lifts us from that war is not a sentiment; it is a transfer of the right to punish to one common power whose judgement replaces all private judgements precisely because it is not one man's conscience but everyone's agreed substitute.

Nothing prevents him. That is the entire argument for the Leviathan.

*Where every man is judge, every man is executioner — and every man is condemned.*
Hume — Judgement:
The question before us is whether "justice" — invoked as warrant for lethal violence — possesses the objective force its claimants assume, or whether it is merely passion wearing the costume of reason.

Custom and sentiment, not abstract principle, are the twin foundations of moral life. When a man declares himself justice's instrument, he mistakes a sentiment peculiarly vivid to himself for a universal law inscribed in nature's fabric. But I have shown that reason alone moves nothing — it is always passion that drives the sword. The zealot and his victim share the same faculty of moral sentiment; they differ only in the objects to which that sentiment is attached. There is no tribunal of Pure Justice above both heads to adjudicate whose sentiment is correct.

Nothing prevents the next man from killing you. Nothing whatsoever.

*When every executioner believes himself Heaven's deputy, justice becomes merely the last man standing.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
The question is not merely about violence but about the corruption that self-love works upon our faculty of moral judgment, transforming private resentment into the costume of universal principle.

When a man appoints himself the executor of justice, he has displaced the impartial spectator — that imagined disinterested observer whose approbation alone confers moral legitimacy — with his own inflamed passions. The very partiality that makes him aggrieved disqualifies him from pronouncing sentence. His adversary, equally convinced of his own rectitude, finds precisely the same warrant in precisely the same reasoning; and so the chain of retribution extends without limit, each link forged from sincere indignation.

Society does not merely prefer formal justice to private revenge — it requires it absolutely, for without the civil magistrate to adjudicate impartially, justice becomes indistinguishable from appetite.

The man who kills for justice has not ended injustice; he has merely enrolled himself in its perpetuation.

*When every man is his own judge, no man can be innocent.*
